examTakeaway: A lens-shaped bleed after a lucid interval is arterial blood from the middle meningeal artery, trapped by sutures.
scenario: A 22-year-old man is hit in the temple. He talks for an hour, then becomes drowsy and one pupil dilates. CT shows a lens-shaped collection that stops at the sutures. There was no slow fall three weeks earlier and the collection does not cross suture lines.
question: Why does the blood form a lens instead of a crescent?
options: Scalp blood stays outside the bone
Suture lines stop an arterial epidural bleed
The transverse sinus is the source
correctAnswer: Suture lines stop an arterial epidural bleed
explanation: A lens-shaped bleed after a lucid interval is arterial blood from the middle meningeal artery, trapped by sutures. Suture lines stop an arterial epidural bleed, so the collection cannot creep into a crescent. Bridging veins ooze across sutures and make a crescent, usually after a slower story. Aneurysm blood fills the cisterns at the moment of the headache. Scalp blood stays outside the bone. The transverse sinus is a venous channel, not this lens.

examTakeaway: The worst headache, a negative CT, and xanthochromia on a later spinal tap are a ruptured berry aneurysm.
scenario: A 49-year-old woman has the worst headache of her life while lifting. CT at two hours shows no blood. A lumbar puncture six hours later shows yellow supernatant that does not clear between tubes. She has adult polycystic kidney disease. There was no temple trauma.
question: Which vessel class ruptured?
options: A carotid dissection in the neck only
The middle cerebral artery stem with a wedge infarct
explanation: The worst headache, a negative CT, and xanthochromia on a later spinal tap are a ruptured berry aneurysm. A berry aneurysm at the circle of Willis is also associated with polycystic kidneys, and yellow fluid that persists across tubes is blood that has sat in the CSF. The middle meningeal artery is an epidural lens after trauma. Bridging veins make a subdural crescent. A carotid dissection in the neck only causes pain and an ischemic sign, not xanthochromia. The middle cerebral artery stem with a wedge infarct is an arterial occlusion, not blood in the spinal fluid.

examTakeaway: Strength that improves after a few steps means more acetylcholine is released with repeated firing, the opposite of a receptor blockade.
scenario: A 61-year-old man with a 30-pack-year history struggles to rise from a chair, then walks better after a few steps. Reflexes return after he grips. CT shows a hilar mass. The eyelids are not the main problem and strength does not fade through the day.
question: Why does repeated use improve the strength?
options: More acetylcholine is released with each firing
correctAnswer: More acetylcholine is released with each firing
explanation: Strength that improves after a few steps means more acetylcholine is released with repeated firing, the opposite of a receptor blockade. More acetylcholine is released with each firing when the attack is on the presynaptic calcium channel, so use helps. The postsynaptic receptor recovers is myasthenia, which worsens with use. A demyelinated nerve catches up is not a use-dependent improvement over a few steps. Botulinum wears off in seconds is false; botulinum paralysis does not improve with grip. The muscle chloride channel opens is myotonia, delayed relaxation.

examTakeaway: Eyelids that droop after sustained gaze have fewer working acetylcholine receptors, so rest restores transmission.
scenario: A 28-year-old woman sees double by evening. The eyelids droop after she looks up for a minute and improve after rest. CT shows an anterior mediastinal mass. Leg strength does not improve with repeated grip. She has no lung cancer.
question: Why does rest restore the eyelids?
options: Presynaptic stores refill after a lung cancer
A demyelinated nerve remyelinates in a minute
Remaining acetylcholine receptors are no longer saturated
correctAnswer: Remaining acetylcholine receptors are no longer saturated
explanation: Eyelids that droop after sustained gaze have fewer working acetylcholine receptors, so rest restores transmission. Remaining acetylcholine receptors are no longer saturated once acetylcholine is cleared, so the few unblocked receptors work again. Presynaptic stores refill after a lung cancer is Lambert-Eaton, which improves with use and tracks a lung mass she does not have. A demyelinated nerve remyelinates in a minute is impossible. Glutamic acid decarboxylase recovers is stiff-person syndrome. A sodium channel reopens is not the myasthenia mechanism.

examTakeaway: A cape of lost pain with spared touch means the crossing spinothalamic fibers were cut, while the dorsal columns sit outside the syrinx.
scenario: A 35-year-old man burned his hands and did not feel it. Pain and temperature are lost over both shoulders. Touch and position sense in the fingers are intact. The legs are spastic. MRI of the neck is ordered. There is no facial pain and no Horner syndrome.
question: Why is touch spared while pain is lost in both arms?
options: Crossing pain fibers were cut and the dorsal columns were spared
The dorsal columns were the only tracts cut
One lateral corticospinal tract explains the cape
A single spinothalamic tract explains both arms
correctAnswer: Crossing pain fibers were cut and the dorsal columns were spared
explanation: A cape of lost pain with spared touch means the crossing spinothalamic fibers were cut, while the dorsal columns sit outside the syrinx. Crossing pain fibers were cut and the dorsal columns were spared, which is a central cord lesion. The dorsal columns were the only tracts cut would lose touch, which is intact. One lateral corticospinal tract explains the cape is wrong; that tract is motor. A single spinothalamic tract explains both arms would cause a contralateral level, not a suspended cape. The optic radiation was cut is a cerebral visual path.

examTakeaway: Bilateral eighth-nerve tumors are a merlin loss on chromosome 22, and the skin-tumor gene is a different protein.
scenario: A 22-year-old woman has hearing loss in both ears. MRI shows a mass on each eighth nerve. She has no cafe-au-lait spots and no optic glioma. Her father had the same tumors. She asks which gene product differs from the one that causes skin fibromas.
question: Which protein is lost in the bilateral-nerve disease?
explanation: Bilateral eighth-nerve tumors are a merlin loss on chromosome 22, and the skin-tumor gene is a different protein. Merlin is the product lost here. Neurofibromin is the skin-fibroma and cafe-au-lait gene she does not have. Hamartin is tuberous sclerosis. Von Hippel-Lindau protein loss causes kidney cancer and cerebellar hemangiomas. Retinoblastoma protein loss causes eye tumors in children.

examTakeaway: Ash-leaf spots and a kidney tumor of fat and vessels mean mTOR is no longer restrained by hamartin-tuberin.
scenario: A 12-year-old boy has pale leaf-shaped patches under a Wood lamp and a seizure. CT shows calcified nodules along the ventricles. Ultrasound shows a renal mass of fat, vessels, and muscle. He has no bilateral eighth-nerve tumors. He asks what the missing complex normally restrains.
question: Which pathway runs too freely?
explanation: Ash-leaf spots and a kidney tumor of fat and vessels mean mTOR is no longer restrained by hamartin-tuberin. mTOR, no longer restrained, drives the nodules and the angiomyolipoma. RAS from neurofibromin loss is NF1, with cafe-au-lait spots and neurofibromas. Hypoxia-inducible factor from VHL loss causes clear-cell kidney cancer and cerebellar hemangiomas, not an angiomyolipoma. A sonic-hedgehog skin tumor is basal cell carcinoma. The dystrophin-actin link is muscle, not this kidney mass.

examTakeaway: A cerebellar hemangioblastoma plus clear-cell kidney cancer means hypoxia-inducible factor is not being destroyed.
scenario: A 30-year-old man has ataxia. MRI shows a cerebellar cyst with a bright nodule. One kidney has a clear-cell carcinoma and the pancreas has cysts. There is no angiomyolipoma and no ash-leaf spot. His mother had a similar kidney cancer. He asks what the missing protein normally marks for disposal.
question: Which factor accumulates when that protein is lost?
explanation: A cerebellar hemangioblastoma plus clear-cell kidney cancer means hypoxia-inducible factor is not being destroyed. Hypoxia-inducible factor accumulates and drives vascular tumors and the kidney cancer. mTOR in tuberous sclerosis fits ash-leaf spots and angiomyolipomas, which he does not have. RAS in NF1 fits skin fibromas. Merlin in the eighth nerve is NF2. Beta-catenin is a colon-cancer pathway, not this family tumor set.

examTakeaway: Failed adduction on lateral gaze with spared convergence means the medial longitudinal fasciculus is demyelinated, because convergence bypasses that tract.
scenario: A 26-year-old woman has had two episodes of blurred vision months apart, each resolving. On left gaze the right eye does not adduct and the left eye has nystagmus. She can still converge. Spinal fluid has oligoclonal bands. MRI shows periventricular white-matter lesions.
question: Why can she converge if she cannot adduct on side gaze?
options: Convergence bypasses the demyelinated connecting tract
The abducens nerve in the orbit is cut
Only the optic nerve is required for convergence
correctAnswer: Convergence bypasses the demyelinated connecting tract
explanation: Failed adduction on lateral gaze with spared convergence means the medial longitudinal fasciculus is demyelinated, because convergence bypasses that tract. Convergence bypasses the demyelinated connecting tract, so near gaze still works. The oculomotor nucleus is destroyed would also lose convergence and the pupil. The abducens nerve in the orbit is cut would fail abduction, not adduction. Only the optic nerve is required for convergence does not move the eye. The corticospinal tract drives convergence is a limb pathway.

examTakeaway: Tongue fasciculations plus spastic legs, with a normal sensory exam, are loss of both upper and lower motor neurons.
scenario: A 58-year-old man has trouble buttoning and then develops a stiff, bouncing gait. The tongue twitches at rest. Reflexes in the legs are brisk and the Babinski signs are upgoing. Sensation is normal and there is no sensory level. MRI of the neck shows no syrinx.
question: Which pair of neurons died?
explanation: Tongue fasciculations plus spastic legs, with a normal sensory exam, are loss of both upper and lower motor neurons. Upper and lower motor neurons die together in ALS, so fasciculations and brisk reflexes coexist and sensation is spared. Dorsal-column neurons only would cost position sense, which is intact. Anterior-horn cells only would weaken and fasciculate without upgoing toes. A demyelinating peripheral nerve would drop the reflexes. The neuromuscular junction fatigues the eyelids and does not cause Babinski signs.

examTakeaway: A brown corneal ring and a low ceruloplasmin mean copper is not being excreted into bile, so it settles in the brain and the liver.
scenario: A 19-year-old man has a new tremor and slurred speech. A brown ring is seen at the edge of the cornea. Ceruloplasmin is low and the liver enzymes are high. Serum iron is normal. There is no family history of a CAG-repeat chorea. He asks where the copper should have left the body.
question: Which route of copper excretion failed?
explanation: A brown corneal ring and a low ceruloplasmin mean copper is not being excreted into bile, so it settles in the brain and the liver. Biliary copper excretion is the failed route. Intestinal iron absorption control fails in hemochromatosis, and his iron is normal. Hepatic bilirubin conjugation fails in Crigler-Najjar syndrome. Canalicular bilirubin excretion fails in Dubin-Johnson syndrome. Pulmonary copper loss is not how copper balance is kept.

examTakeaway: Behavior failing before memory, with frontal atrophy, means the poles degenerated before the cholinergic memory neurons.
scenario: A 58-year-old man has become rude, overeats sweets, and ignores his family. Recent memory is relatively spared. MRI shows severe frontal and temporal atrophy and relative sparing of the parietal lobe. There is no resting tremor. He asks why memory is not the first loss.
question: Which neurons fail first in this pattern?
explanation: Behavior failing before memory, with frontal atrophy, means the poles degenerated before the cholinergic memory neurons. Frontal and temporal pole neurons fail first, so manners go before memory. Nucleus basalis cholinergic neurons are the Alzheimer loss, which hits memory first and the parietal lobe. Substantia nigra loss is a resting tremor he does not have. Mammillary bodies are an acute confusional state in poor nutrition. The caudate is Huntington disease, with chorea.
